"It's a David-versus-Goliath scenario... at some point, we'll find a weak spot and strike there," said FNSPF spokesman Eric Brocardi. French president Emmanuel Macron will hold a crisis cabinet meeting to discuss the emergency on Monday morning. Spanish prime minister Pedro Sanchez will visit fire-hit areas in Valencia, in the east of the country, on Monday, where firefighters are battling a new blaze and where 15,000 people have been forced to flee their homes. On Sunday, during a visit to the fire zone in Avila province west of Madrid, he warned: "Difficult hours lie ahead." Spain's interior minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said Sunday evening the fires were advancing, but slowly. Earlier Sunday, civil protection chief Virginia Barcones, describing the fire around Avila, said the country was battling a "monster". "We are dealing with a perimeter of 280km encompassing 77,000 hectares (190,000 acres)," Barcones told state broadcaster TVE of the wildfire. 'Extremely intense' Scientists say climate change is making such extreme weather events more frequent and intense. Coming at the height of the summer holiday season, the fires were fuelled by woodland parched to tinder by successive heatwaves and lack of rain since May. In France, the prefect of the southwestern Gironde region, where the country's fires are concentrated, urged tourists to stay away and seek "other destinations". Around 220,000 people have been evacuated in the region, with 45 campsites forced to shut, ruining the holiday plans of around 40,000 people. Garden hose in hand, Georges Clivaz sprayed water along a road leading to his property in Saint-Jean-d'Illac as the blaze burned a few kilometres away. "We're doing this to slow down the fire's advance; we want to save our homes," he told AFP. Although the village was evacuated on Friday, Clivaz said he and his family were trying to hold out. "But the firefighters are telling us that in two or three hours the fire will be here." Interior minister Laurent Nunez warned "the situation remains very unfavourable" across France, where more than 250,000 people have been evacuated. The main fire in Gironde, home to Bordeaux, was "extremely intense and unpredictable... generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area", he said on X. Firefighters injured Since Wednesday, the fire in the Gironde region has injured 84 firefighters, 10 of whom have been evacuated, according to the latest situation report published Sunday by the prefecture. Sebastien Bouvier, federal secretary of France's CFDT union, said firefighters lacked adequate protective equipment against the fires' toxic fumes. Weather forecasters warn another heatwave could hit France from Tuesday, with temperatures reaching 40C in some areas. At least 240 homes have been destroyed in Gironde region, many of them in village Le Porge. But Bordeaux mayor Thomas Cazenave said there were no plans to evacuate the city's urban area, home to 850,000 people and sheltering thousands displaced by the fires. Local officials remained "vigilant", he added. The fire has ravaged 42,000 hectares in Gironde - an area seven times the size of Manhattan, since Wednesday. France's defence ministry said it has taken special steps to protect industrial sites around Bordeaux, a key centre of the country's aerospace industry. The main freeway south of Bordeaux and rail services have been cut. Some 2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel and around 1,200 police have been deployed to the Gironde region. 'Incalculable' damage King Felipe VI, visiting an emergency shelter in Villamanta on Madrid's western outskirts, said the wildfires had caused "incalculable" damage to Spain's natural heritage. Around 75,000 residents have been evacuated from the Madrid region, Avila, Toledo and from the eastern region of Castellon in Valencia. "We had a real scare," said Azucena Paguada, one of those evacuated to the Villamanta gym-turned-shelter. "The Guardia Civil came to our house and made us leave, telling us we were in danger." Another evacuee, 70-year-old Margarita, showed the stains on her T-shirt, which she has been wearing for four days. "The queen came to say hello, and I was wearing this dirty thing," she added with a sigh. Officials said winds were pushing wildfires near Madrid to the south, away from the capital for now, but forcing more evacuations of villages in their path. Hundreds of kilometres away, the new Valencia fire was proving "very intense", Pilar Bernabe, the central government delegate to Valencia, wrote on X. One person was killed on Saturday in a separate, smaller fire near Valencia, the only civilian death so far reported in the wildfires. In France, two firefighters were killed near Bordeaux on Tuesday. Pope Leo IV, in his prayers on Sunday, expressed solidarity with all those affected by the "devastating" Spanish and French fires and called on people to pray for them and first responders. Italy, too, was facing its own fires. More than 400 tourists and beachgoers were evacuated by sea near the town of Peschici in the southern Puglia region, with 300 more expected to be rescued, said the coastguard.

article_annotations.title: France, Spain battle ‘monster’ wildfires with more heat on the way | Kuwait Times Newspaper
article_annotations.source_independence_reason: Kuwait Times 文末署 AFP；Free Malaysia Today 的正文大段同文并指明 AFP 采访。
article_annotations.content:
BORDEAUX: Firefighters battled massive blazes tearing through forests across France and Spain Monday, as authorities warned of a fresh heatwave set to engulf the scorched French wine-growing region around the major city of Bordeaux. More than 325,000 people have fled their homes, mostly in the Gironde department, home to Bordeaux, as some of the worst forest fires in either country’s history rage across southwest France and central Spain near Madrid.

France’s fire has caused an unprecedented “pyrocumulonimbus”—a giant fire cloud that creates its own winds and packs lightning that causes more blazes, said the National Firefighters Federation of France (FNSPF).

“It’s a David-versus-Goliath scenario... at some point, we’ll find a weak spot and strike there,” said FNSPF spokesman Eric Brocardi. French President Emmanuel Macron will hold a crisis cabinet meeting to discuss the emergency on Monday morning.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez will visit fire-hit areas in Valencia, in the east of the country on Monday where firefighters are battling a new blaze and where 15,000 people have been forced to flee their homes. On Sunday, during a visit to the fire zone in Avila province west of Madrid, he warned: “Difficult hours lie ahead.”

Spain’s Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said Sunday evening the fires were advancing, but slowly. Earlier Sunday, civil protection chief Virginia Barcones, describing the fire around Avila, said the country was battling a “monster”. “We are dealing with a perimeter of 280 kilometres encompassing 77,000 hectares (190,000 acres),” Barcones told state broadcaster TVE of the wildfire.

Scientists say climate change is making such extreme weather events more frequent and intense. Coming at the height of the summer holiday season, the fires were fuelled by woodland parched to tinder by successive heatwaves and lack of rain since May.

In France, the prefect of the southwestern Gironde region and where the country’s fires are concentrated, urged tourists to stay away and seek “other destinations”. “The wind is changing so much, it’s really the fire calling the shots. We just have to go with it,” a firefighter said.

Around 220,000 people have been evacuated in the region, with 45 campsites forced to shut, ruining the holiday plans of around 40,000 people.

The Gironde local authority said early Monday it had banned holiday camps, including Scouts’ trips involving overnight stays and holiday camps for people with disabilities. Garden hose in hand, Georges Clivaz sprayed water along a road leading to his property in Saint-Jean-d’Illac in Gironde as the blaze burned a few kilometres away.

“We’re doing this to slow down the fire’s advance; we want to save our homes,” he told AFP. Although the village was evacuated on Friday, Clivaz said he and his family were trying to hold out. “But the firefighters are telling us that in two or three hours the fire will be here.”

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned “the situation remains very unfavourable” across France, where more than 250,000 people have been evacuated. The Gironde local authority said early Monday, though, that the fire had remained “broadly stable” overnight.

Since Wednesday, the fire in the Gironde area has injured 84 firefighters, 10 of whom have been evacuated, according to the latest situation report published Sunday by the prefecture. Sebastien Bouvier, federal secretary of France’s CFDT union, said firefighters lacked adequate protective equipment against the fires’ toxic fumes.

Weather forecasters warn another heatwave could hit France from Tuesday, with temperatures reaching 40C in some areas. At least 240 homes have been destroyed in Gironde region, many of them in village Le Porge.

But Bordeaux mayor Thomas Cazenave said there were no plans to evacuate the city’s urban area, home to 850,000 people and sheltering thousands displaced by the fires. Local officials remained “vigilant”, he added. The fire has ravaged 42,000 hectares in Gironde—an area seven times the size of Manhattan, since Wednesday.

France’s defence ministry said it has taken special steps to protect industrial sites around Bordeaux, a key centre of the country’s aerospace industry. The main freeway south of Bordeaux and rail services have been cut. Some 2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel and around 1,200 police have been deployed to the Gironde region.

King Felipe VI, visiting an emergency shelter in Villamanta on Madrid’s western outskirts, said the wildfires had caused “incalculable” damage to Spain’s natural heritage. Around 75,000 residents have been evacuated from the Madrid region, Avila, Toledo and from the eastern region of Castellon in Valencia.

“We had a real scare,” said Azucena Paguada, one of those evacuated to the Villamanta gym-turned-shelter. “The Guardia Civil came to our house and made us leave, telling us we were in danger.”

Another evacuee, 70-year-old Margarita, showed the stains on her T-shirt, which she has been wearing for four days. “The queen came to say hello, and I was wearing this dirty thing,” she added with a sigh. Officials said winds were pushing wildfires near Madrid to the south, away from the capital for now, but forcing more evacuations of villages in their path.

Hundreds of kilometres away, the new Valencia fire was proving “very intense”, Pilar Bernabe, the central government delegate to Valencia, wrote on X. A separate, smaller fire near Valencia killed one person on Saturday, the only civilian death reported so far in the wildfires. In France, two firefighters died near Bordeaux on Tuesday. Pope Leo IV, in his prayers on Sunday, expressed solidarity with all those affected by the “devastating” Spanish and French fires and called on people to pray for them and first responders.

Italy, too, was facing its own fires.

More than 400 tourists and beachgoers were evacuated by sea near the town of Peschici in the southern Puglia region, with 300 more expected to be rescued, said the coastguard. — AFP

article_annotations.title: A human-made forest is at the centre of France''s raging wildfires
article_annotations.source_independence_reason: 明确 CBC 现场访谈及记者 Anna Cunningham 的署名图片。
article_annotations.content:
For days after she and her partner were evacuated from their apartment in Lège-Cap-Ferret, Naomie Corsaint and her family tried to find out what happened to the house they'd lived in for a decade in nearby Le Porge, where a forest fire raged.

Photos and videos trickled in, mostly from firefighters already hard at work.

The 20-year-old didn't get to see the scale of the devastation until she was granted permission to visit the community on Sunday. When she arrived, she saw only the cinder walls of her mother's house were left.

"The town we used to know is gone," Corsaint told CBC on Tuesday.

"You can’t even get your bearings anymore; the houses we used to see when driving by — there’s nothing left. It’s all ash."

Corsaint and her family are among the more than 250,000 people evacuated from their homes in France as fires spread at an unprecedented rate near Bordeaux . In Spain, more than 116,000 people have had to leave their communities as fires continue to burn there, too.

Scientists say climate change is the primary driver behind the extraordinary fire conditions gripping western Europe, with a fourth heat wave of the season settling over the region this week.

But they also say the scale of the fires cannot be understood without looking at how humans transformed the landscape itself.

Château La Rochefoucauld is seen northwest of Bordeaux earlier this month in a photo taken by CBC reporter Anna Cunningham on the banks of a dried-up river. (Anna Cunningham/CBC)

The pine forest stretching southwest of Bordeaux has long been one of France's great engineering success stories.

In the mid-1800s, under Napoleon III, vast wetlands considered unhealthy and unproductive were drained and replaced with a pine forest. The new forest transformed the local economy, produced timber and resin and made the area habitable.

Nearly two centuries later, that same landscape is burning.

"This isn't a fire in a natural forest," said Raphaël Morera, an environmental historian at the French National Centre for Scientific Research, in an interview. "It’s a fire in a forest that was planted there to support an industrial activity."

Morera says natural forests tend to contain a greater diversity of tree species and more interruptions that can slow a fire's advance.

In the Landes, by contrast, "there are no natural obstacles to the fire's expansion," leaving firefighters to do almost all the work of stopping it.

While France's firefighters are among the best equipped in Europe, the fires themselves are changing faster than emergency services can adapt, says Guillermo Rein, a professor of fire science at Imperial College London.

What's more, European countries rely on each other for labour and equipment, but when fires rage in many countries at once, that becomes more difficult, especially with aging Canadair tanker fleets .

Amid successive heat waves and months of unusually dry conditions, the landscape has lost much of the moisture that normally helps limit fire behaviour, according to Sylvain Delzon, a forest ecophysiologist at the University of Bordeaux and France's National Research Institute for Agriculture, Food and Environment.

"It's a sandy soil that doesn't retain water. So all the undergrowth was completely dried out and dead, becoming fuel for the fire."

In terms of scale and spread, the fires in France share some similarities with the 2016 Horse River Fire that prompted the evacuation of Fort McMurray in Alberta, said Stefan Doerr, a professor of wildfire science at Swansea University in Wales.

Drone video shows homes reduced to ashes, rubble by wildfire in southwestern France

"In both cases the fire behaviour is quite extreme," Doerr said in a video interview, noting the fires in France have created their own weather system — a phenomenon that also occurred around Fort McMurray, with the fire creating its own high winds and lightning .

This week, images of a gigantic black cloud above France spread online. The cloud, a pyrocumulonimbus , is composed of the moisture evaporated from burnt trees and vegetation, in addition to soot particles. It is formed by the energy and heat created by large forest fires pushing the air into the sky.

To Corsaint, whose family home in Le Porge burned, and her boyfriend, Mattéo Martins, 21, the results were "almost apocalyptic."

Before the couple had to leave their apartment in Lège-Cap-Ferret last week, they watched as the sky around them turned black.

"All we could see was smoke. Ash fell on the balcony," Corsaint said. "Then, at night, the sky was orange and red. You could hear planes, police sirens, everything except other people."

You can only see these fire clouds during huge wildfires

Trump says Canada should stop wildfire smoke. Experts say it's not that simple

Sophie Wilkinson, a wildfire and peatland researcher at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia who studied the Alberta wildfire — where there were also drained wetlands — said climate change is exposing the legacy of earlier land-use decisions.

"The era of denialism and pushing climate change into the future as a future issue is really gone."

Europe’s wildfires are creating their own weather systems

Wilkinson, speaking in a phone interview Tuesday, said extreme heat, drought and wildfire are symptoms of human-caused climate change, adding that protecting and restoring ecosystems such as peatlands must also be part of the response.

Susan Page, professor of physical geography at the University of Leicester in England who has spent decades studying peatlands, echoed Wilkinson's comments.

"I think it's right that we now — rather than talking about climate change — talk about climate breakdown," Page said.

"That's what we're starting to see, because the fires that are happening in France and Spain are of a scale that we never imagined."

Naomie Corsaint says her mother and step-father have been crying every day over their lost home, which had also served as her mom's workplace.

In their town, roughly 150 others saw their houses burn down. Corsaint and Martins know it will take months to rebuild. And they worry that once the headlines die down, people will forget.

"None of it feels real," she said.

"In both cases the fire behaviour is quite extreme," Doerr said in a video interview, noting the fires in France have created their own weather system — a phenomenon that also occurred around Fort McMurray, with the fire creating its own high winds and lightning .

This week, images of a gigantic black cloud above France spread online. The cloud, a pyrocumulonimbus , is composed of the moisture evaporated from burnt trees and vegetation, in addition to soot particles. It is formed by the energy and heat created by large forest fires pushing the air into the sky.

To Corsaint, whose family home in Le Porge burned, and her boyfriend, Mattéo Martins, 21, the results were "almost apocalyptic."

Before the couple had to leave their apartment in Lège-Cap-Ferret last week, they watched as the sky around them turned black.

"All we could see was smoke. Ash fell on the balcony," Corsaint said. "Then, at night, the sky was orange and red. You could hear planes, police sirens, everything except other people."

fact_spans.span_text:
You can only see these fire clouds during huge wildfires

Trump says Canada should stop wildfire smoke. Experts say it's not that simple

Sophie Wilkinson, a wildfire and peatland researcher at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia who studied the Alberta wildfire — where there were also drained wetlands — said climate change is exposing the legacy of earlier land-use decisions.

"The era of denialism and pushing climate change into the future as a future issue is really gone."
Europe’s wildfires are creating their own weather systems

Wilkinson, speaking in a phone interview Tuesday, said extreme heat, drought and wildfire are symptoms of human-caused climate change, adding that protecting and restoring ecosystems such as peatlands must also be part of the response.

Susan Page, professor of physical geography at the University of Leicester in England who has spent decades studying peatlands, echoed Wilkinson's comments.

"I think it's right that we now — rather than talking about climate change — talk about climate breakdown," Page said.

"That's what we're starting to see, because the fires that are happening in France and Spain are of a scale that we never imagined."

Naomie Corsaint says her mother and step-father have been crying every day over their lost home, which had also served as her mom's workplace.

In their town, roughly 150 others saw their houses burn down. Corsaint and Martins know it will take months to rebuild. And they worry that once the headlines die down, people will forget.

"None of it feels real," she said.
